name: Peshok
tagline: Tea slopes above the meeting of the Teesta and the Rangeet
meta_description: Peshok on a budget: Lovers' Meet viewpoint over the Teesta–Rangeet confluence, the Lepcha legend, Peshok and Lopchu tea, jeep fares and tea-village homestays.
summary: Peshok is a tea-garden village about 30 km from Darjeeling on the road down to Teesta Bazar and Kalimpong, at roughly 1,000–1,200 m. From the Lovers' Meet viewpoint you look down on the confluence of the Teesta and the Rangeet. Shared Darjeeling–Kalimpong jeeps pass through; homestays cost about ₹1,500–2,500 with meals.

local_story.title: Rongnyu, Rongeet and the meeting below Peshok
paras: Below the tea slopes of Peshok, two rivers come together. The Teesta runs down from North Sikkim; the Rangeet comes from the west, draining the slopes of Kanchenjunga and the Singalila range, and forms part of the boundary between Darjeeling and Sikkim before it ends. They meet near Melli and Teesta Bazar at a spot often called Triveni. From the road above, at a viewpoint that locals and drivers call Lovers' Meet, you look straight down on the junction.

The name comes from a Lepcha story, and we tell it as folklore. Lepcha elders say the two rivers, Rongnyu (the Teesta) and Rongeet (the Rangeet), were lovers who agreed to meet in the plains below. Rongnyu chose a serpent as her guide, and it led her by the most direct way, so she arrived first. Rongeet followed a bird, which wandered and stopped to feed, so he came late and hurt to find her already waiting. The story is told in several versions, but the meeting of the two rivers is always its heart.

The hillside itself is tea country. Peshok tea estate covers the slopes around the village, and Lopchu, one of the better-known gardens of the Darjeeling hills, lies close by on the same road. The road through both, from Ghoom and Jorebunglow down to Teesta Bazar, is the main link between Darjeeling and Kalimpong, so Peshok has long watched the traffic of the hills pass by its tea rows. Tea here grows lower and warmer than in the high gardens around Darjeeling town.

did_you_know: In Lepcha the Teesta is called Rongnyu and the Rangeet Rongeet; the Lovers' Meet viewpoint above Peshok is named after the folk tale of the two rivers as lovers.
Peshok lies on the main Darjeeling–Kalimpong road through Ghoom, Jorebunglow, Lopchu and Teesta Bazar, so shared jeeps between the two towns pass through the village.
The Rangeet forms part of the boundary between Darjeeling district and Sikkim along its lower course before it joins the Teesta below Peshok, near Melli.
intro: Peshok is a stop most people pass at 40 km an hour on the way from Darjeeling to Kalimpong. That is a pity, because it is one of the most useful half-days on the Darjeeling side of the Teesta. In a short drive from Darjeeling you drop roughly 1,000 m from the cold ridge at Ghoom into warm tea country, with the deep valleys of the Teesta and the Rangeet opening below. The air smells of tea and wet earth, and the light on the slopes in late afternoon is lovely.

We suggest it as a half-day or day trip combined with Lamahatta, or as one or two quiet nights in a tea-village homestay before you carry on to Kalimpong. Stand at Lovers' Meet, walk the garden paths in plucking season and buy Peshok or Lopchu tea close to where it grows. The road below Teesta Bazar has had serious damage and long closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood, so check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Lovers' Meet viewpoint
highlights.text: A roadside viewpoint looking down on the meeting of the Teesta and the Rangeet near Melli and Teesta Bazar. On clear days you can follow both rivers back into their valleys. Come in the morning before the valley haze rises; by afternoon it is often a blur.

highlights.title: The Lepcha tale of two rivers
highlights.text: The Lepcha story of Rongnyu and Rongeet, the river lovers who took different guides to their meeting, gives the viewpoint its name. Read it before you go; it makes the shape of the valley below far more interesting than a plain river junction.

highlights.title: Peshok tea estate
highlights.text: Tea slopes run steeply down from the road on all sides. From roughly March to November you can watch pluckers at work in the rows, and the garden paths make a pleasant hour's walk. Ask before entering the estate and stay on the paths.

highlights.title: Lopchu, next door
highlights.text: Lopchu, a short way up the same road, is one of the better-known names in Darjeeling tea, sold widely in the hills and the plains. Buy a packet nearby, and compare its dark, rounded cup with the lighter teas from gardens higher up.

highlights.title: The road from Ghoom to the Teesta
highlights.text: The drive from Ghoom through Jorebunglow, past Lamahatta and Lopchu to Peshok, drops through conifer forest, village terraces and tea. Sit on the valley side for long views. It is also the classic route between Darjeeling and Kalimpong.

highlights.title: Quiet nights in a tea village
highlights.text: A night in one of the village homestays around the garden shows you the tea workers' side of the hills: early starts, simple meals, and evenings of tea and talk. It is warmer than Darjeeling and cheaper than town hotels.

how_to_reach.text: Darjeeling–Kalimpong shared jeeps run through Peshok, leaving from the Darjeeling motor stand when full, about 1–1.5 hours to Peshok. You will usually be charged close to the full Kalimpong fare of ₹200–250. Getting back is harder: wave down a passing jeep with space, which can take time in the afternoon.

The easiest way to see Lovers' Meet, Lamahatta and Peshok's tea in one go. A car from Darjeeling for a half-day or day circuit costs about ₹2,500–3,500. Drivers know the viewpoint by name. Combine with Kalimpong as a one-way transfer if you are moving on.

You can come up via Sevoke and NH10 to Teesta Bazar and then climb to Peshok, roughly 70 km, or go round via Darjeeling. NH10 along the Teesta has had long closures and damage since the October 2023 flood, so many drivers prefer to come up via Darjeeling. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There are no named properties at Peshok we can recommend with confidence, so we describe the area instead. Small family homestays are scattered through the tea-garden villages around Peshok and Lopchu, usually about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, often with valley views. Lamahatta, on the same road towards Darjeeling, has many more village homestays and makes a good base for Peshok as a day trip. Teesta Bazar below has simple riverside lodges if you are heading on to Kalimpong. Ask about hot water and road access, especially in the monsoon.
tips: Go to Lovers' Meet in the morning; valley haze usually hides the confluence after midday.
If you rely on shared jeeps, plan the return before you get off, as passing jeeps are often full in the afternoon.
Combine Peshok with Lamahatta on the same road for a full, easy day from Darjeeling.
Ask before walking into the tea estate or photographing pluckers, and keep to the paths between rows.
Check the status of NH10 and the Teesta Bazar road before planning a route down to the valley.

experiences.title: Lovers' Meet and the Teesta–Rangeet confluence
experiences.summary: Stand above the meeting of the Teesta and the Rangeet at the Lovers' Meet viewpoint on the Peshok road, and hear the Lepcha tale of the two river lovers who chose different guides for their journey.
body: The Lovers' Meet viewpoint sits on the road between Peshok and Teesta Bazar, looking down into the deep valley where the Rangeet joins the Teesta near Melli. The Teesta comes down from North Sikkim; the Rangeet from the west, out of the high country around Kanchenjunga and the Singalila range. From the railing you can trace both rivers back up their valleys on a clear morning. Below the junction the joined river carries on south towards the plains.

The name comes from Lepcha folklore. The local story is that Rongnyu (the Teesta) and Rongeet (the Rangeet) were lovers who agreed to meet in the plains. Rongnyu followed a serpent, which took her the straight way, and she arrived first. Rongeet followed a bird that dawdled, so he arrived late and hurt. Tellings differ in detail, but this junction is where they are said to have met. Tell it to children on the way down; they remember it.

Come in the morning between October and April for the clearest view; afternoon haze often flattens the valley into a grey blur, and in the monsoon cloud can hide it entirely. The viewpoint is small and roadside, with a railing and space for a few cars, so allow half an hour and combine it with Lamahatta or a tea walk. Cars pull in all day in season, so the quietest time is early. Binoculars help you pick out the two rivers' different colours where they meet and the settlements along the valley floor.

faqs.q: Where is Lovers' Meet near Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Lovers' Meet is a roadside viewpoint on the Darjeeling–Kalimpong road between Peshok and Teesta Bazar, about 30 km from Darjeeling. It looks down on the confluence of the Teesta and the Rangeet near Melli. Any Darjeeling driver knows it by name, and shared Kalimpong jeeps pass right by.

faqs.q: Why is it called Lovers' Meet?
faqs.a: The name comes from a Lepcha folk tale. The rivers Rongnyu (Teesta) and Rongeet (Rangeet) were lovers who agreed to meet in the plains. Rongnyu followed a serpent and arrived first; Rongeet followed a bird that dawdled and came late. The viewpoint looks down on the place where the two rivers join.

faqs.q: Can you see the two rivers in different colours?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Where they meet, the Teesta and the Rangeet can look different in colour for a stretch, depending on season, rain and silt upstream. The contrast is usually clearest in the dry months from November to March. After heavy rain both turn brown and the difference fades.

experiences.title: Morning walk through Peshok's tea rows
experiences.summary: Walk the paths of Peshok tea estate in the cool of the morning, when pluckers are working the rows. Steep slopes, valley views and a close look at how Darjeeling tea is picked, two leaves and a bud.
body: Peshok tea estate spreads over the slopes around the village, falling steeply towards the Teesta valley. Like all registered gardens in these hills, its tea can carry the Darjeeling name, a protected Geographical Indication since 2004. The garden paths, used by workers every day, let you walk between the rows with long views down the valley. Peshok is lower and warmer than the gardens around Darjeeling town, and its slopes face the Teesta valley, which gives the walk its long views.

Come early. From roughly March to November pluckers start in the morning, moving along the rows with baskets on their backs and taking the top two leaves and a bud. First flush is picked in spring, second flush in early summer, and monsoon and autumn flushes later. In winter the bushes are pruned and rest. Pluckers' days are long, so keep your questions short and do not hold them up.

Ask at the roadside or a homestay before entering the estate, stay on the paths, and ask before photographing workers. Factory visits are not a regular tourist service, as far as we know, so do not count on one. Carry water and wear shoes with grip; garden paths are steep and slippery when wet. In the rains, leeches appear in the rows, so tuck trousers into socks from June to September.

faqs.q: Can I walk inside Peshok tea garden?
faqs.a: Visitors commonly walk the paths of tea gardens along this road, but the estate is private working land. Ask at the roadside, a shop or your homestay before going in, stay on the paths between rows and do not pick leaves. Avoid the factory area unless you are invited.

faqs.q: Is there a factory tour at Peshok?
faqs.a: We do not know of a regular public factory tour at Peshok, so treat it as a garden walk. For a guided look at withering, rolling and drying, Happy Valley Tea Estate near Darjeeling town is the more reliable choice. Ask locally, as policies at individual estates can change.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see tea plucking at Peshok?
faqs.a: From March to November, in the morning. March and April bring first flush, May and June the second flush, and July to October the monsoon and autumn flushes. From December to February the bushes are pruned and resting, so the slopes are quiet but still good for walks.

experiences.title: An evening in a tea-village homestay
experiences.summary: Spend a night with a family in one of the tea-garden villages around Peshok and Lopchu. Watch the valley lights come on, eat a home-cooked hill dinner and wake to pluckers heading for the rows.
body: Most visitors see Peshok through a jeep window. A night in a village homestay shows you the people who make the tea. Many families in these villages have worked in the gardens for generations, and their houses stand on the slopes between the tea rows. Rooms are simple and clean, meals are eaten with or near the family, and the evenings are quiet. Valley lights come on below as it gets dark, and on clear nights the stars are bright.

Dinner is usually rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable, a green, pickle and, if you ask in advance, chicken or eggs. Breakfast might be puri with potato curry. Tea, of course, comes all day. Ask your hosts about the garden: plucking seasons, how the work is paid, how the village has changed. Most are happy to talk if you are interested and not hurried. Eat what is offered, as meals are cooked fresh for you, and if you like a dish, say so; it is the best compliment.

Book through a Darjeeling agent or by phone before you come; there are no walk-in signboards for many homestays, and some houses are a short walk down from the road on garden paths. Confirm hot water, the walk from the road to the house and whether the family can meet you at the roadside when your jeep drops you. Carry a torch, as paths between houses are unlit. Pay in cash at the end of the stay, and if you buy tea from the family or neighbours, ask which garden and flush it comes from.

faqs.q: Are there homestays in Peshok?
faqs.a: Yes, small family homestays are scattered through the tea-garden villages around Peshok and Lopchu, usually at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Most are booked by phone or through Darjeeling agents rather than online. Lamahatta, on the same road, has many more homestays if Peshok is full.

faqs.q: Is Peshok warmer than Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes. At roughly 1,000–1,200 m Peshok sits about 900–1,000 m below Darjeeling, so days are noticeably warmer and winter nights milder. You still need a sweater or light jacket from November to February, but not the heavy layers you need at Ghoom or Tiger Hill.

faqs.q: What should I bring for a tea-village homestay?
faqs.a: Cash for the stay and any tea you buy, a torch for the path after dark, shoes with grip, a light jacket and insect repellent in the warmer months. Tell your hosts in advance about dietary needs. Mobile signal can be weak away from the main road.

experiences.title: Ghoom to Teesta Bazar by the Peshok road
experiences.summary: Drive the classic road from Ghoom down to Teesta Bazar: Jorebunglow, Lamahatta's prayer flags, Lopchu and Peshok's tea, the Lovers' Meet view, then the river. A drop of nearly 2,000 m in a few hours.
body: Ghoom stands on a saddle at about 2,258 m where the roads of the Darjeeling hills divide. One of them heads east through Jorebunglow and drops towards the Teesta. On the way down it passes conifer forest and village terraces, the dhupi trees and prayer flags of Lamahatta, the tea of Lopchu and Peshok, and the Lovers' Meet viewpoint, before reaching the river at Teesta Bazar, a few hundred metres above sea level.

It is the main road between Darjeeling and Kalimpong, so you can ride it by shared jeep for about ₹200–250, or hire a car and stop wherever you like. Sit on the valley side. Take a sweater for the top and a T-shirt for the bottom; the change in temperature is striking. Lunch at Teesta Bazar, where simple eating houses serve rice meals and momos, before you carry on or turn back up the hill.

Teesta Bazar and the valley roads below it have suffered from landslides and the October 2023 Teesta flood, with long closures on NH10 between Sevoke and Rangpo. Before you plan to continue to Kalimpong, Gangtok or Siliguri this way, check current status before you travel. The climb from Teesta Bazar back up to Darjeeling is slow in the afternoon, when jeeps and trucks stack up on the hairpins, so leave time. In the monsoon, add buffer hours to any plan, and avoid driving the valley roads after dark.

faqs.q: How long is the drive from Darjeeling to Kalimpong via Peshok?
faqs.a: About 50 km and 2.5–3 hours by shared jeep or car, through Ghoom, Jorebunglow, Lopchu, Peshok and Teesta Bazar. Shared jeeps cost about ₹200–250 a seat. Landslides and repairs in the Teesta valley can lengthen the trip, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Teesta Bazar road open after the 2023 flood?
faqs.a: The road from Darjeeling down to Teesta Bazar has generally been used for Darjeeling–Kalimpong traffic, but NH10 along the Teesta has seen long closures and damage since October 2023. Conditions change with rain and repair work. Ask your driver or the jeep stand on the day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stop at Lamahatta and Lovers' Meet in one trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Both lie on the same Darjeeling–Kalimpong road, Lamahatta higher up and Lovers' Meet below Peshok. With a reserved car for about ₹2,500–3,500 you can see both, walk some tea paths and be back in Darjeeling by mid-afternoon, or carry on to Kalimpong.

faqs.q: Where is Peshok?
faqs.a: Peshok is a tea-garden village on the Darjeeling–Kalimpong road, about 30 km from Darjeeling, between Lopchu and Teesta Bazar. It sits at roughly 1,000–1,200 m above the Teesta valley. The Lovers' Meet viewpoint, looking down on the Teesta–Rangeet confluence, is on the road just below.

faqs.q: What is Peshok famous for?
faqs.a: Peshok is known for its tea estate and for the Lovers' Meet viewpoint over the confluence of the Teesta and the Rangeet, named after a Lepcha folk tale of two river lovers. Lopchu, a well-known Darjeeling tea garden, is next door on the same road.

faqs.q: How do I reach Peshok from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Take a Darjeeling–Kalimpong shared jeep and ask to get off at Peshok or Lovers' Meet, about 1–1.5 hours; you will usually pay close to the full ₹200–250 Kalimpong fare. A reserved car for a half-day or day circuit with Lamahatta costs about ₹2,500–3,500.

faqs.q: Is Peshok worth a visit?
faqs.a: Yes, as a half-day or day trip, especially combined with Lamahatta. The views into the Teesta and Rangeet valleys, the Lepcha story behind Lovers' Meet and the tea slopes make a good change from Darjeeling's town sights. Stay a night only if you want a quiet tea-village homestay.

faqs.q: What is the Lepcha legend of the Teesta and the Rangeet?
faqs.a: Lepcha elders tell that the rivers Rongnyu (Teesta) and Rongeet (Rangeet) were lovers who agreed to meet in the plains. Rongnyu followed a serpent by the straight way and arrived first. Rongeet followed a bird that wandered, and he arrived late and hurt. Versions differ, but the confluence below Peshok is their meeting place.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Peshok?
faqs.a: Peshok is mainly a valley viewpoint rather than a mountain one. The best views here are down into the Teesta and Rangeet valleys and across to the Kalimpong hills. For Kanchenjunga on the same road, go up to Lamahatta, where the peaks show on clear mornings, or to Tiger Hill near Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Are there places to stay in Peshok?
faqs.a: Yes, a few family homestays in the tea-garden villages around Peshok and Lopchu, usually ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. We do not name individual properties as we cannot vouch for them. Lamahatta nearby has more choice, and Teesta Bazar has simple lodges for travellers heading on to Kalimpong.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Peshok?
faqs.a: October to December for clear valley views, and March and April for tea plucking and spring green. Winters are milder than in Darjeeling. Avoid June to September: rain, haze and landslides on the Teesta valley roads make views poor and travel slow.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive to Teesta Bazar from Peshok?
faqs.a: The road is narrow and steep but well used by jeeps and buses every day. The risk comes from landslides in the monsoon and damage since the October 2023 Teesta flood, which has closed sections of NH10 for long periods. Travel in daylight and check current status before you travel.
